The short answer

WordbitX websites start at Rs. 20,000 on your own domain and hosting, or Rs. 25,000 with a domain and one year of hosting. Market estimates are PKR 30,000–60,000 for a basic freelancer build, PKR 60,000–150,000 for a small agency, and PKR 150,000–350,000+ for an established agency.
Compare scope before comparing prices

A five-page brochure and a booking platform are not the same purchase. A brochure explains your business and sends enquiries to your phone. A booking platform also stores appointments, checks availability and handles changes. Write down which one you need before requesting a price. WordbitX’s starter scope covers 5–10 pages, a CMS, basic SEO and three months of support. Confirm the final page list in your written quote. Extra languages, unusual layouts and external systems need their own scope.
What the two published packages mean

The Rs. 20,000 starting price assumes you bring your own domain and hosting. The Rs. 25,000 starting price adds domain registration and hosting for one year. Do not add a made-up hosting subscription to either package. WordbitX does not publish standalone hosting plans. Renewal starts at Rs. 10,000 per year for the all-in-one arrangement. Ask which domain extension, storage limits, backup policy and renewal services are included before you pay.
Why market quotes look different

A freelancer may have fewer overheads but less backup when unavailable. An agency may include planning, design review and a separate tester. Neither business model guarantees quality. Ask every supplier to price the same pages, contact forms, content entry and handover. Check whether copywriting, real photography, paid plugins and migration are included. A lower price can be fair when the scope is smaller; it becomes misleading when necessary work is hidden until launch.
The cheapest advertised website

Competitors advertise websites from PKR 5,000. Offers under PKR 10,000–15,000 usually mean a copied template with weak security and no support; inspect the actual terms rather than judging on price alone. Do not assume every low-cost developer is dishonest. Ask about licensed themes, updates, backups and access ownership. WordbitX is not claiming to be the cheapest in Pakistan. Its published package is a comparison point, not proof that another supplier cannot suit you better.
Write a brief that a supplier can actually price

Start with the business problem rather than a list of fashionable technologies. Explain who will use the system, what they need to finish and what happens after they submit information. Include the pages or workflows needed for the first version, the content you already have and any service that must connect to it. Remove private customer records from example files. A clear brief does not have to be long, but it should tell two suppliers enough to price the same job. If a feature is optional, label it optional rather than letting it silently become part of the essential launch.
Ask for a written scope and a fair comparison

Request a quote that separates implementation from recurring services and later changes. Confirm currency, tax treatment, billing periods and what happens when a third-party provider changes its terms. Market ranges are planning estimates, not an invoice or a promise that your project will fit the lowest figure. Ask what is excluded as carefully as what is included. Compare the same deliverables across suppliers and record assumptions in one place. You can then choose a smaller first release deliberately rather than discovering after payment that important work was outside the original scope.
Agree acceptance checks before work begins

Describe what a working result looks like in plain words. A visitor should be able to find the right service, submit a valid enquiry and understand what happens next. Staff should have the right permissions and a safe way to correct mistakes. Use realistic content and ordinary mobile devices during review. Check missing fields, failed requests and recovery paths as well as the happy path. These checks help both sides recognise completion and reduce arguments about whether a feature was technically present but practically unusable. Keep a short record of approvals and outstanding issues.
Plan handover and ongoing responsibility

Know who owns each account, who receives renewal messages and who responds if something stops working. Request access to the relevant domain, hosting, repository and administrative tools, with appropriate security. Do not exchange passwords in public documents. Ask for a handover checklist and basic instructions for regular staff tasks. Support should explain which fixes are included and which new features need another quote. Three months of launch support is not the same as unlimited future development. Review access when a contractor leaves so that the business can keep operating safely.

Use the first conversation to clarify requirements, not to accept an invented deadline or an unverified discount. If a supplier needs more information before quoting, that can be responsible scoping rather than avoidance. Ask for the unanswered questions in writing and decide who will provide each answer. Keep the first launch focused enough to test and maintain. Once you have real usage evidence, prioritise the next improvements. A sensible plan makes room for uncertainty without pretending that every price, launch date or business result can be guaranteed before the work has been understood.
Check the real cost after the first year

Before making a decision, create a simple list of everything that renews: domains, hosting, subscriptions, extensions and any agreed maintenance. Record who pays each bill and what happens if you cancel. Ask whether the introductory rate changes at renewal and whether you can export your content and records. Keep copies of invoices and the agreed scope with the business owner. This makes it easier to compare an inexpensive first year with a more stable ongoing arrangement.
